title: Сложные предложения и причастные обороты / Complex sentences and participle constructions
bridge: In Russian, relative and subordinate clauses are often condensed using active and passive participles, whereas in Spanish this is resolved with constructions like 'que + verb' or 'siendo + participle'. This structural difference is key: Russian prefers a nominal phrase with a participle where Spanish uses a relative clause. Additionally, Russian participles agree in gender, number, and case with the noun they modify, which requires special attention from Spanish speakers.
rule: Russian participles (действительные и страдательные) are formed from verbs and function as adjectives. For imperfective verbs, present forms are used (-ущий/-ющий, -емый/-имый), and for perfective verbs, past forms are used (-вший, -нный/-тый). They agree with the noun in gender, number, and case. Active participles: читающий (who reads), прочитавший (who read); passive participles: читаемый (read, which is being read), прочитанный (read). At C1 level, it is essential to master the full forms without shortening (short forms exist only for passive participles in predicate). Additionally, the Russian participle can indicate relative time: a present participle refers to simultaneity, while a past participle refers to anteriority. Many subordinate clauses with 'который' can and often are replaced by participles for greater conciseness, which is common in written and formal colloquial style.

concept_examples.text: Книга, читаемая студентом, лежит на столе.
concept_examples.translation: The book that is being read by the student is on the table.

concept_examples.text: Мы встретили женщину, рассказывавшую о путешествии.
concept_examples.translation: We met the woman who was telling about the trip.

concept_examples.text: Написанное письмо было отправлено вчера.
concept_examples.translation: The written letter was sent yesterday.

concept_examples.text: Студенты, сдавшие экзамен, получили высокие оценки.
concept_examples.translation: The students who passed the exam received high grades.

common_error.wrong: Студент, читающий книгу, сидел за столом, и он пил чай, и он говорил с другом.
common_error.correct: Студент, читающий книгу и пьющий чай, разговаривал с другом.
common_error.correct_alt: Студент, сидевший за столом и читавший книгу, разговаривал с другом.
common_error.explanation: Spanish speakers tend to chain coordinated clauses with 'и' (and) in Russian, mimicking Spanish structure. At C1 level, Russian prefers compacting ideas using participles or gerunds to reduce excessive subordination. Use participles to describe simultaneous or sequential actions about the same noun, thus avoiding repetitive use of 'и' and relative pronouns.

examples.translation: the student who reads
examples.note: Active present participle of the verb 'читать' (to read). Agrees in gender, number, and case.

examples.translation: the issues being discussed
examples.note: Passive present participle: indicates an action being performed on the noun.

examples.translation: We discussed issues related to ecology.
examples.note: The participle 'касающиеся' (related to) requires the genitive case, as does the original verb 'касаться' (to relate to).

examples.translation: the book read (that was read)
examples.note: Passive past participle of the verb 'прочитать' (to read). Used to describe an object affected by a past action.

examples.translation: the snow that has melted
examples.note: Active past participle of the verb 'растаять' (to melt). Indicates a past action performed by the noun itself.

examples.original: Построенный в прошлом году мост уже используется.
examples.phonetic: [pɐˈstro(j)ɪnːɨj f ˈproʂləm ɡɐˈdu most ʊʐɨ ˈispəlʲzʊ(j)ɪt͡sə]
examples.translation: The bridge built last year is already in use.
examples.note: The passive past participle is frequently used to describe objects or results of completed actions.

levels.label: Participial phrases and synonymy with subordinate clauses
levels.translation: Participial phrases and synonymy with subordinate clauses

examples.original: Студента, не сдавшего экзамен, попросили прийти на пересдачу.
examples.phonetic: [stʊˈdʲɛntə nʲɪ ˈzdafʂɨvə ɪkˈzamʲɪn, pəprɐˈsʲilʲɪ prʲɪjˈtʲi nə pʲɪrʲɪzˈdat͡ɕʊ]
examples.translation: The student who did not pass the exam was asked to come for a retake.
examples.note: The participle 'не сдавшего' (who did not pass) is in the genitive case, agreeing with the direct object 'студента'.

examples.original: Я прочитал статью, написанную известным учёным.
examples.translation: I read the article written by a famous scientist.
examples.note: Here, the passive past participle can replace the subordinate clause 'которую написал учёный'. The agent is placed in the instrumental case.

examples.original: Посмотрев фильм, я решил прочитать книгу.
examples.translation: After watching the film, I decided to read the book.
examples.note: This example introduces the gerund (деепричастие), related to participles, to express prior actions in a compact manner.

translations.en: Advanced syntax: complex sentences and participle constructions

title: Регистр и стиль: формально, неформально, нейтрально / Register and style: formal, informal, neutral
bridge: In Spanish, register is marked by the use of tú/usted, the subjunctive, and certain formulas. In Russian, the distinction is much sharper: it manifests in the choice of pronouns (ты/вы), in the selection of syntactic constructions, and in specific vocabulary. Unlike Spanish, where politeness often softens the register, in Russian excessive use of polite forms can sound artificial or sarcastic. Additionally, verbs of politeness and impersonal constructions vary much more than in Spanish. The main challenge for a Spanish speaker is knowing when to use second-person plural verb forms with a capital letter (Вы) and when to omit the pronoun, as well as recognizing impersonal constructions that in Spanish would be expressed with 'se'.
rule: In Russian, register is defined by three axes: the level of formality (formal/informal), the relationship between speakers (symmetry/asymmetry of power), and the medium (oral/written). 1) Tú/usted: 'ты' (informal 'you') is used with friends, family, children, and in informal contexts among equals. 'вы' (formal 'you') is used with strangers, in formal situations, and when there is social distance. Writing 'Вы' with a capital letter in official correspondence marks special respect. 2) Impersonal constructions: in formal register, impersonal forms are preferred such as 'следует отметить' (it should be noted), 'необходимо' (it is necessary), 'представляется целесообразным' (it seems appropriate). In informal register, personal forms are used: 'надо', 'мне кажется' (it seems to me). 3) Vocabulary: there are pairs of similar words but with different registers, such as 'есть' (to eat, neutral) vs 'кушать' (to eat, more polite or used with children, but sounds affected in first person) and 'работать' vs 'трудиться' (to work, more formal or literary). 4) Syntax of politeness: in formal register, direct questions are avoided, and the conditional form is used ('Не могли бы вы...?' – Could you...?), while in informal register, direct imperatives or questions with the particle 'ли' are used. 5) In written register, participles and adverbs such as 'соответственно' (respectively) and 'следовательно' (therefore) are used, which are less common in speech. It is crucial not to mix registers: using 'вы' with singular verb forms (usted) while using plural verb forms (vosotros) is a common error. In Russian, when using informal 'ты', verbs are in the second-person singular; when using 'вы' with a respectful meaning (usted), verbs are in the second-person plural, but gender forms remain masculine/feminine according to the interlocutor. There is no exact equivalent of the impersonal 'se' in Spanish; instead, constructions with 'нужно' (it is needed), 'можно' (it is possible) or reflexive verb forms are used.

concept_examples.text: Извините, вы не подскажете, где находится библиотека?
concept_examples.translation: Excuse me, could you tell me where the library is?
concept_examples.phonetic: [izvʲi'nʲitʲe, vɨ nʲə pɐtsˈkaʐɨtʲe, ɡdʲe nɐˈxodʲɪtsə bʲɪblʲɪɐˈtʲekə]

concept_examples.text: Слушай, ты не знаешь, где тут библиотека?
concept_examples.translation: Hey, do you know where the library is around here?
concept_examples.phonetic: [ˈsluʂəj, tɨ nʲɪ ˈznajɪʂ, ɡdʲe tut bʲɪblʲɪɐˈtʲekə]

concept_examples.text: Следует отметить, что данная проблема требует незамедлительного решения.
concept_examples.translation: It should be noted that this problem requires an immediate solution.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ˈslʲedʊjɪt ɐtˈmʲetʲɪtʲ, ʂtə ˈdanːəjə prɐˈblʲemə trʲɪˈbujɪt nʲɪzəmʲɪdˈlʲitʲɪlʲnəvə rʲɪˈʂɛnʲɪjə]

concept_examples.text: Мне кажется, нам надо это обсудить.
concept_examples.translation: It seems to me that we need to discuss this.

common_error.wrong: Вы можете помочь мне с этим? (using 'Вы' but with the singular verb 'можете' is correct, but the common error is mixing: 'Ты можете помочь мне?' – incorrect because it mixes 'ты' with the conjugation of 'вы'). The most typical error among Spanish speakers is: 'Мне нужно, чтобы вы помогли мне' in an informal context, or using 'кушать' in the first person singular (I eat) as 'Я кушаю' in a neutral register, when it sounds affected.
common_error.correct: Вы можете помочь мне с этим? (formal) or Ты можешь помочь мне с этим? (informal)
common_error.correct_alt: Не могли бы вы мне помочь с этим? (formal, more polite) or Можешь помочь? (informal direct)
common_error.explanation: The error arises because in Spanish 'tú' and 'usted' share many conjugations (usted come, tú comes), but in Russian the distinction is clearer: 'ты' is only used with second-person singular verbs (можешь), while 'вы' is used with second-person plural verbs (можете). Mixing both produces a grammatical error. Another common error is using the form 'кушать' (to eat) in the first person, which in Russian sounds childish or pretentious; the neutral form is 'есть'. To avoid these errors, it is best to learn verb conjugations in pairs (ты/вы) and memorize register collocations, such as 'можно' vs 'разрешите' (allow me).

examples.original: Уважаемый Иван Петрович, позвольте выразить благодарность за сотрудничество.
examples.phonetic: [ʊvɐˈʐajɪmɨj ɪˈvan pʲɪˈtrovʲɪtɕ, pɐzˈvolʲtʲe vɨˈrazʲɪtʲ bləɡɐˈdarnəsʲtʲ zə sətrʊdʲnʲɪˈt͡ɕestvə]
examples.translation: Dear Ivan Petrovich, allow me to express my gratitude for your collaboration.
examples.note: In formal letters, the name and patronymic (Иван Петрович) are used, not just the surname, and 'позвольте' (allow me) is used for politeness.

examples.original: Предлагается рассмотреть данный вопрос на следующем заседании.
examples.phonetic: [prʲɪdɐˈɡaɪtsə rəsːmɐˈtrʲetʲ ˈdanːɨj vɐˈpros nə ˈslʲedʊjʉɕːɪm zəsʲɪˈdanʲɪɪ]
examples.translation: It is proposed to consider this matter at the next meeting.
examples.note: Use of the passive construction with '-ся' (предлагается) and impersonal structure, typical of formal register.

examples.translation: Hi! How are you? What's new?
examples.note: The greeting 'привет' is informal and not used with strangers. In formal situations, 'здравствуйте' is used.

examples.original: Слушай, не хочешь сходить в кино вечером?
examples.phonetic: [ˈsluʂəj, nʲɪ ˈxot͡ɕɪʂ sxɐˈdʲitʲ f kʲɪˈno ˈvʲet͡ɕɪrəm]
examples.translation: Hey, do you feel like going to the cinema this evening?
examples.note: Use of the imperative 'слушай' to get attention, and the colloquial 'не хочешь' (literally 'don't you want') with the meaning of an invitation.

examples.translation: Yesterday we went to the theater.
examples.note: This statement is neutral, with no formal or informal markers. It is the standard register in everyday conversation.

examples.original: Нужно заполнить анкету и отправить её в отдел кадров.
examples.phonetic: [ˈnuʐnə zɐˈpolnʲɪtʲ ɐnˈkʲetʊ i ɐtˈpravʲɪtʲ jɪˈjɵ v ɐˈdʲel ˈkadrəf]
examples.translation: You need to fill out the form and send it to the HR department.
examples.note: Use of 'нужно' (it is needed) for impersonal constructions, neutral, common in instructions.

translations.en: Register and style: formal, informal, and neutral

title: Инверсия и выдвижение в начало / Inversion and Frontalization (Advanced)
bridge: In Spanish, word order is relatively flexible, but inversion is typically limited to questions or emphasis with intonation. In Russian, inversion and frontalization are fundamental syntactic mechanisms that mark theme and rheme (known vs. new information), without relying on intonation. Unlike Spanish, where the subject usually precedes the verb, in Russian the order can be freely altered to emphasize any element, and this often combines with postpositioning of the subject. Spanish speakers tend to maintain the SVO order when translating, losing crucial pragmatic nuances.
rule: In Russian, word order is pragmatic: known information (theme) goes at the beginning, and new information (rheme) at the end. Frontalization involves placing an element (object, complement, adverb) at the start of the sentence to emphasize it or to connect with prior discourse. Inversion, on the other hand, places the verb before the subject, which usually indicates that the subject is rheme or that the event is presentational. At the C1 level, mastery of constructions such as: (1) Object + verb + subject (e.g., «Эту книгу я прочитал» – emphasis on the object), (2) Adverb + verb + subject (e.g., «Здесь живёт мой брат» – presentational), and (3) Use of particles like «и» or «же» to enhance the fronted element is expected. There are no strict rules, but the choice depends on the discourse context. Common errors include translating literally from Spanish, ignoring the theme/rheme distribution, or using inversion in contexts where it sounds archaic or poetic.

concept_examples.text: Эту книгу я прочитал ещё в детстве.
concept_examples.translation: Este libro lo leí ya en mi infancia.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈɛtʊ ˈknʲiɡʊ ja prətɕɪˈtal jɪˈɕːo v ˈdʲetstvʲe

concept_examples.text: На столе лежит свежий хлеб.
concept_examples.translation: Sobre la mesa hay pan fresco.

concept_examples.text: Только сейчас я понял свою ошибку.
concept_examples.translation: Solo ahora comprendí mi error.
concept_examples.phonetic: ˈtolʲkə sʲɪjˈtɕas ja ˈponʲɪl svɐˈju ɐˈʂɨpkʊ

concept_examples.text: В этом городе он провёл всю жизнь.
concept_examples.translation: En esta ciudad él pasó toda su vida.
concept_examples.phonetic: v ˈɛtəm ˈɡorədʲɪ on prɐˈvʲol fsʲu ʐɨzʲnʲ

common_error.wrong: Я прочитал эту книгу ещё в детстве.
common_error.correct: Эту книгу я прочитал ещё в детстве.
common_error.correct_alt: Эту книгу я ещё в детстве прочитал.
common_error.explanation: This error is typical because in Spanish the neutral order is SVO, and when emphasizing the object, intonation or constructions like 'lo que... es...' are usually used. In Russian, to highlight 'this book', it is placed at the beginning (fronting). If the SVO order is maintained, the sentence sounds neutral and the emphasis is lost. To avoid this, consider which element is the new information (rheme) and place it at the end; the rest goes before.

examples.translation: Esta película la he visto dos veces.
examples.note: The direct object is placed at the beginning to emphasize it. In Spanish, the duplicated object pronoun 'la' is often used.

examples.translation: La carta la escribió ayer.
examples.note: Frontalization of the object without duplication is common in Russian; in Spanish the pronoun is necessary.

levels.label: Инверсия с обстоятельствами места и времени
levels.translation: Inversion with adverbials of place and time

examples.translation: En el parque juegan niños.
examples.note: Inversion with the verb before the subject presents new information (the children). It is equivalent to 'there are children playing'.

examples.translation: Mañana llegará mi hermano.
examples.note: The temporal adverb at the beginning and the subject after the verb are natural in Russian; in Spanish it sounds formal or poetic.

examples.translation: En la habitación había una mesa vieja.
examples.note: Presentational inversion is used to describe existence or presence.

examples.original: Именно это я имел в виду.
examples.phonetic: ˈimʲɪnːə ˈɛtə ja ɪˈmʲel v vʲɪˈdu
examples.translation: Precisamente eso quería decir.
examples.note: The particle «именно» reinforces the fronted element, equivalent to 'precisely' or 'just'.

examples.translation: A nadie vi allí.
examples.note: Frontalization of a negative pronoun with inversion is emphatic; in Spanish double negation is used.

examples.translation: ¡Él sí aceptó de inmediato!
examples.note: The particle «же» after the fronted element adds contrast or surprise.

title: Сложная номинализация: процесс → действие / Complex nominalization: process → action
bridge: In Russian, the nominalization of processes is typically achieved with suffixes like -ение/-ание, while Spanish uses suffixes like -ción, -miento or -da. However, Russian maintains the verbal aspect in the noun (perfective/imperfective), something that does not exist in Spanish. Additionally, Russian verbal nouns retain the original verb's government (required case), which often leads to case errors if the Spanish speaker transfers the prepositional structure of Spanish directly. For example, 'управление чем' vs. 'gestión de algo' — in Russian the instrumental case is used, not the genitive.
rule: In Russian, the nominalization of processes (verbs → nouns) is formed with productive suffixes: -ение (from -ить verbs: читать → чтение, управлять → управление), -ание (from -ать verbs: выступать → выступление, but also -ание: рисовать → рисование), -тие (from -ять/-иять: открыть → открытие), and -ка (colloquial, deverbal nouns: стирка, покраска, but with a nuance of concrete action). The noun inherits the aspectual government of the verb: if the verb governs instrumental, genitive, dative or accusative, the noun requires the same case (управление проектом — instrumental, достижение цели — genitive, помощь другу — dative). There is no universal 'de' preposition in Russian; possessive or object relationships are expressed with genitive, but the differential verbal government is maintained. For processes, the imperfective aspect is preferred (чтение, а не прочтение — which refers to the completed action). For results, the perfective aspect is used (решение — decision/resolution, достижение — achievement). Nominalization allows the construction of genitive chains: 'управление процессами развития' (management of development processes), where the plural genitive is used for the plural direct object. Typical errors by Spanish speakers include always using genitive for the object (влияние на что vs. влияние на что — correct with accusative), omitting the governed case, or confusing aspect: 'сдача экзамена' (the process of taking an exam) vs. 'сдать экзамен' (to complete the exam). At C1 level, the use of nominalizations in academic and business registers is expected, including derivatives with prefixes (пере- переработка, до- доработка, вы- выступление).

concept_examples.text: Чтение книг развивает мышление.
concept_examples.translation: Reading books develops thinking.

concept_examples.text: Управление проектом требует опыта.
concept_examples.translation: Managing the project requires experience.

concept_examples.text: Достижение целей связано с усилием.
concept_examples.translation: Achieving goals is related to effort.

concept_examples.text: Обработка данных занимает много времени.
concept_examples.translation: Data processing takes a lot of time.

common_error.explanation: The error arises because the Spanish speaker translates 'gestión de proyecto' using the genitive case (проекта) as in Spanish 'de'. However, the noun 'управление' inherits the government of the verb 'управлять', which requires the instrumental case (кем? чем?). Thus, it must be 'управление проектом'. To avoid this error, it is essential to identify the case governed by the original verb and maintain it in the noun, rather than mechanically using the genitive.

examples.translation: Reading books is useful.
examples.note: The suffix -ение is added to the present tense stem of the verb (чита- + -ние). In Spanish, 'lectura' does not require a preposition, but in Russian the direct object is put in the genitive case (книг) because the noun is deverbal.

examples.translation: Drawing develops creativity.
examples.note: -ание is used for verbs ending in -ать (рисовать). Learn to identify the verbal stem and add the corresponding suffix.

examples.translation: Time management is a key skill.
examples.note: Note that 'временем' is in the instrumental case, required by 'управлять'. Do not use the genitive here.

examples.translation: Taking the exam requires preparation.
examples.note: Here 'сдача' refers to the process of taking the exam (imperfective aspect). The genitive 'экзамена' is correct because 'сдать' governs the accusative, but when nominalized, the object becomes genitive.

examples.translation: The solution to the problem has been found.
examples.note: Here 'решение' refers to the result (perfective aspect). The genitive 'проблемы' is correct here because it is a direct object in the genitive, not because of government.

examples.translation: The discussion of the plan lasted an hour.
examples.note: The distinction between process and result can be subtle. Here 'обсуждение' is a process, and the genitive 'плана' is normal (the verb 'обсудить' governs the accusative, but the nominalization uses genitive for the object).

examples.translation: Managing development processes requires strategy.
examples.note: A chain is observed: 'процессами' in the instrumental case (due to government), 'развития' in the genitive case (noun complement). In Spanish we use 'de' for everything, but here the instrumental case is maintained.

examples.translation: Research into the impact of changes on society.
examples.note: The noun 'влияние' governs the preposition 'на' + accusative (на общество). You cannot use 'влияние общества' with genitive for the object. This is a point of contrast with Spanish.

examples.translation: Improving employee qualifications is an important task.
examples.note: Here 'повышение' governs the genitive (квалификации), and then 'сотрудников' is a plural genitive possessive. The chain of genitives is common, but the governed object must be distinguished.

title: Эллипсис и субституция / Ellipsis and substitution
bridge: In Spanish, we use pronouns like 'lo', 'so', 'neither' (influenced by English) or verbal ellipsis ('yo también', 'nosotros tampoco') to avoid repetition. In Russian, ellipsis is much more flexible: the verb is often omitted when the context makes it clear, and substitution is done using particles like 'тоже' (also), 'так же' (the same way) or 'и я' (and I). The typical mistake of Spanish speakers is to translate 'so do I' literally as 'так делаю я' instead of using the appropriate Russian structure, which often only employs 'и я' or 'я тоже'. Additionally, Russian does not have a direct equivalent of 'so' or 'neither' as substitution pronouns; instead, it relies on complete predicate ellipsis, keeping only the subject or object.
rule: In Russian, verb ellipsis (пропуск) is common in short answers and in coordinating sentences. To express agreement or coincidence with a previous statement, 'тоже' (also) or 'и' + personal pronoun in the same grammatical case as the omitted subject is used. The typical structure is: [nominative subject] + 'тоже' (or 'и я', 'и мы', etc.) without repeating the verb, since it is implied by the context. For negations, 'тоже не' or 'и я не' (me neither) is used. 'Так же' is also used to mean 'in the same way'. The structures 'so do I' or 'neither have we' from English are not used; in Russian, the auxiliary verb and often the direct object are omitted, leaving only the particle and the subject. In coordinated sentences, verb ellipsis in the second clause is mandatory if the verb and tense are the same, and the direct object can also be omitted if it is identical. At C1 level, students are expected to use these structures in both formal and colloquial speech and to distinguish between 'тоже' (coincidence) and 'также' (in addition), as well as between 'и я' (and I) and 'я тоже' (me too) in different registers.

concept_examples.text: Я люблю кофе, и она тоже.
concept_examples.translation: I like coffee, and she does too.

concept_examples.text: Он не пришёл, и я не.
concept_examples.translation: He didn’t come, and neither did I.

concept_examples.text: Мы уже видели этот фильм, а они — нет.
concept_examples.translation: We’ve already seen this movie, and they haven’t.
concept_examples.phonetic: [mɨ uˈʐɨ ˈvʲidʲɪlʲɪ ˈɛtət ˈfʲilʲm, a ɐˈnʲi — nʲet]

concept_examples.text: Она говорит по-русски, и он так же.
concept_examples.translation: She speaks Russian, and he does too (in the same way).
concept_examples.phonetic: [ɐˈna ɡɐˈvɐrʲɪt pɐ ˈruskʲɪ, i on tak ʐɛ]

common_error.wrong: Я тоже так делаю, как он. (literal translation of 'I do so too')
common_error.correct: Я делаю так же, как он.
common_error.explanation: The error occurs because in Spanish, 'también' + verb is used to express coincidence, and the student transfers this to Russian by unnecessarily adding 'так делаю' (I do it that way). In Russian, ellipsis allows omitting the verb if it has already been mentioned, so the natural phrasing is 'Я тоже' or 'Я так же'. To compare ways of doing something, 'так же, как' (the same way as) is used, not 'тоже'.

examples.original: — Ты пойдёшь на вечеринку? — Да, я тоже.
examples.phonetic: [tɨ pɐjˈdʲɵʂ nə vʲɪt͡ɕɪˈrʲinkʊ? — da, ja ˈtoʐə]
examples.translation: — Are you going to the party? — Yes, I am too.
examples.note: In the response, the verb 'пойду' (I will go) is omitted because it is implied by the context; 'тоже' expresses coincidence.

examples.original: — Он не любит дождь. — И я не.
examples.phonetic: [on nʲɪ ˈlʲʉbʲɪt doʂtʲ. — i ja nʲe]
examples.translation: — He doesn’t like the rain. — Neither do I.
examples.note: For negations, 'и я не' (and I don’t) is used without repeating the verb. This is common in colloquial speech.

examples.original: Он пишет стихи, и она тоже.
examples.translation: He writes poems, and she does too.
examples.note: 'тоже' substitutes the verb and object when they are identical. 'пишет стихи' is not repeated.

examples.original: Она готовит вкусно, и он так же.
examples.phonetic: [ɐˈna ɡɐˈtovʲɪt ˈfkusnə, i on tak ʐɛ]
examples.translation: She cooks well, and he does too (in the same way).
examples.note: 'так же' implies 'in the same way', not just coincidence; it is used to compare actions or qualities.

examples.original: Мария читает книги, а Пётр — газеты.
examples.translation: María reads books, and Pyotr, newspapers.
examples.note: The verb 'читает' is omitted in the second clause because it is implied. The dash (—) replaces the omitted verb.

examples.original: Я не люблю опаздывать, а они — тем более.
examples.phonetic: [ja nʲɪ ˈlʲʉblʲʊ ɐˈpazdɨvətʲ, a ɐˈnʲi — tʲɪm ˈbolʲɪə]
examples.translation: I don’t like being late, and neither do they (even less so).
examples.note: 'тем более' is an emphatic expression that replaces 'don’t like' and adds reinforcement. It is typical of C1 level.

title: Маркеры дискурса для продвинутой связности / Discourse markers for advanced cohesion
bridge: In Russian, advanced cohesion relies heavily on particles and connectors that don't have a direct equivalent in Spanish. For example, «ведь» expresses an evident or shared justification, while «же» emphasizes contrast or opposition within the same sentence. Unlike Spanish, where we often use adverbs or phrases (e.g., 'en efecto', 'por cierto'), Russian integrates these nuances into particles that modify the tone and informative structure. Another important trap is that «при этом» can mean 'at the same time' or 'however' depending on the context, something that doesn't happen with a single marker in Spanish.
rule:
Advanced discourse markers in Russian are classified into several categories:

1. **Justification and evidence**: «ведь» (since, because it's evident) is used at the beginning or in the middle of a clause to introduce a reason the speaker assumes is known or accepted. Ex.: «Он не пришёл, ведь он был болен» (He didn't come, since he was sick).

2. **Contrast and emphasis**: «же» (however, on the other hand, precisely) is placed after the word to be emphasized. It can indicate contrast with what was said before or surprise. Ex.: «Я хочу кофе, а она же — чай» (I want coffee, and she, on the other hand, tea).

3. **Additive and temporal connection**: «при этом» (at the same time, however) links two actions that occur simultaneously or present a contrast. Ex.: «Он много работает, при этом находит время для семьи» (He works a lot and, at the same time, finds time for his family).

4. **Reformulation and clarification**: «иными словами» (in other words), «точнее» (more precisely), «вернее» (rather). These are used as in Spanish to correct or specify what was said.

5. **Conclusion and summary**: «итак» (so, in summary), «в итоге» (in the end), «словом» (in a word).

**Practical rules for C1**:
- «ведь» should never be translated as 'porque' in all contexts; it introduces a known or shared cause, not a new one.
- «же» has no fixed equivalent in Spanish; its function is pragmatic: it places focus on the preceding element.
- «при этом» requires context verification: whether it indicates simultaneity or contrast. In Spanish, 'at the same time' and 'however' are mutually exclusive; in Russian, the same marker covers both.
- Do not confuse «итак» (so) with «так» (this way).
- In formal registers, «следовательно» (therefore) is preferred over «итак».

concept_examples.text: Он опоздал на встречу, ведь у него была важная причина.
concept_examples.translation: He arrived late to the meeting, since he had an important reason.
concept_examples.phonetic: [on ɐˈpazdəl nɐ ˈfstrʲet͡ɕʊ, vʲetʲ ʊ nʲɪˈvo ˈbɨlɐ ˈvaʐnəjə prʲɪˈt͡ɕinə]

concept_examples.text: Мы решили остаться дома, при этом погода была прекрасная.
concept_examples.translation: We decided to stay home, despite the weather being beautiful (lit. and at the same time the weather was beautiful).
concept_examples.phonetic: [mɨ rʲɪˈʂɨlʲɪ ɐˈstat͡sə ˈdomə, prʲi ˈetəm pɐˈgodə ˈbɨlə prʲɪˈkrasnəjə]

concept_examples.text: Ты говоришь, что устал, я же вижу, что ты полон энергии.
concept_examples.translation: You say you're tired, whereas I see you're full of energy.
concept_examples.phonetic: [tɨ ɡɐˈvorʲɪʂ, ʂto ʊˈstal, ja ʐɛ ˈvʲiʐʊ, ʂto tɨ ˈpolən ɪˈnɛrɡʲɪɪ]

concept_examples.text: Иными словами, мы не можем позволить себе эту ошибку.
concept_examples.translation: In other words, we cannot afford this mistake.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ɪˈnɨmʲɪ ˈslovəmʲɪ, mɨ nʲɪ ˈmoʐɨm pəzvɐˈlʲit͡sʲ ˈsʲebʲe ˈɛtʊ ɐˈʂɨpkʊ]

common_error.wrong: Он не пришёл, потому что он был болен, ведь это было известно.
common_error.correct: Он не пришёл, ведь он был болен.
common_error.correct_alt: Он не пришёл, потому что он был болен.
common_error.explanation: The error lies in using «ведь» together with «потому что», creating redundancy. In Spanish, 'porque' and 'pues' are sometimes combined, but in Russian «ведь» already implies a shared cause; adding «потому что» is unnecessary and sounds artificial. To avoid this error, decide whether the cause is new (use «потому что») or shared (use «ведь»). Do not combine them.

examples.original: Он не пришёл, ведь у него была срочная работа.
examples.phonetic: [on nʲɪ prʲɪˈʂol, vʲetʲ ʊ nʲɪˈvo ˈbɨlə ˈsrot͡ɕnəjə rɐˈbotə]
examples.translation: He didn't come, since he had urgent work.
examples.note: «ведь» introduces a reason the interlocutor likely already knows or accepts; in Spanish 'pues' may work, but not always.

examples.original: Именно поэтому мы отказались от этого предложения.
examples.phonetic: [ˈimʲɪnːə pɐˈɛtəmʊ mɨ ɐtkɐˈzalʲɪsʲ ɐt ˈɛtəvə prʲɪdlɐˈʐɛnʲɪjə]
examples.translation: Precisely for that reason, we rejected this offer.
examples.note: «именно поэтому» emphasizes the cause directly; in Spanish 'precisely for that reason'.

examples.original: Она молода, при этом очень опытна.
examples.translation: She is young, but very experienced (lit. and at the same time very experienced).
examples.note: «при этом» in this context indicates concession/contrast; it should not be translated literally as 'with this'.

examples.original: Ты говоришь одно, я же утверждаю обратное.
examples.phonetic: [tɨ ɡɐˈvorʲiʂ ɐdˈno, ja ʐɛ ʊtvʲɪrˈʐdajʊ ɐˈbratnəjə]
examples.translation: You say one thing, I, on the other hand, affirm the opposite.
examples.note: «же» places focus on 'я' and establishes a direct contrast with what was said before.

examples.original: Итак, мы подытожили все аргументы и готовы к решению.
examples.phonetic: [ɪˈtak, mɨ pədɨˈtoʐɨlʲɪ fsʲe ɐrɡʊˈmʲentɨ i ɡɐˈtovɨ k rʲɪˈʂɛnʲɪjʊ]
examples.translation: So we have summarized all the arguments and are ready for the decision.
examples.note: «итак» is used to introduce a conclusion after reasoning; equivalent to 'so' or 'in summary'.

examples.original: Точнее, мы не отказались, а отложили это на потом.
examples.phonetic: [ˈtot͡ɕnʲɪjə, mɨ nʲɪ ɐtkɐˈzalʲɪsʲ, a ɐtɫɐˈʐɨlʲɪ ˈɛtə nə pɐˈtom]
examples.translation: More precisely, we didn't reject it, but rather postponed it for later.
examples.note: «точнее» is used to correct or specify; unlike 'more precisely', it is frequently used in conversation.

examples.original: Словом, ситуация сложная, но не безнадёжная.
examples.translation: In a word, the situation is complicated, but not hopeless.
examples.note: «словом» summarizes everything said previously; in Spanish 'in a word'.

title: Смягчение и хеджирование / Softening and Hedging Language
bridge: In Spanish, we use verbs like 'creo que', 'me parece que', 'quizás' and the subjunctive to soften statements. In Russian, there is no direct equivalent to the subjunctive, but multiple constructions with modal particles (бы, вряд ли, пожалуй), introductory verbs and the conditional form are used instead. The challenge for Spanish speakers lies in the fact that Russian expresses uncertainty in a more compact way and often with flexible word order that changes the nuance. Avoid translating 'yo creo que' literally as 'я думаю что' in contexts where Russian would prefer an impersonal construction or a modal particle.
rule: At a C1 level, Russian uses several strategies to express softening and hedging: 1) Modal particles: 'пожалуй' (perhaps, probably), 'вряд ли' (hardly, unlikely), 'едва ли' (barely), 'будто' (as if), 'как будто' (as if), 'словно' (as if), 'якобы' (allegedly). 2) Impersonal constructions: 'мне кажется' (it seems to me), 'мне думается' (it occurs to me), 'следует отметить' (it should be noted), 'можно сказать' (one could say). 3) The conditional with 'бы' (often with 'кажется', 'хотелось бы', 'стоило бы'). 4) Introductory verbs with negation or doubt: 'сомневаюсь, что' (I doubt that), 'не уверен, что' (I'm not sure that), 'предположим' (let's assume). 5) The use of mood (indicative vs. conditional) and word order inversion to emphasize doubt. There is no direct correspondence to the Spanish subjunctive; Russian often uses the indicative after expressions of doubt, though the conditional with 'бы' is used for counterfactual hypotheses. Remember that 'вряд ли' and 'едва ли' are placed at the beginning or after the subject, and that 'пожалуй' is more colloquial.

concept_examples.text: Вряд ли он придёт завтра.
concept_examples.translation: Difícilmente venga mañana.

concept_examples.text: Мне кажется, это решение не совсем верное.
concept_examples.translation: Me parece que esta solución no es del todo correcta.
concept_examples.phonetic: [mnʲe ˈkaʐɨt͡sə ˈɛtə rʲɪˈʂɛnʲɪje nʲɪ sɐˈfsʲɛm ˈvʲɛrnəjə]

concept_examples.text: Пожалуй, я соглашусь с тобой.
concept_examples.translation: Quizás esté de acuerdo contigo.

concept_examples.text: Он как будто не понимает, о чём идёт речь.
concept_examples.translation: Él como si no entendiera de qué se trata.
concept_examples.phonetic: [on kɐɡ ˈbudtə nʲɪ pənʲɪˈmaɪt | ɐ ˈt͡ɕɵm ˈidʲɵt rʲet͡ɕ]

common_error.wrong: Я думаю, что он вряд ли придёт.
common_error.explanation: In Spanish, it is common to combine 'creo que' + 'difícilmente' to soften a statement, but in Russian 'я думаю, что' with 'вряд ли' is redundant and sounds unnatural. 'Вряд ли' already expresses doubt or improbability, so it does not need an introductory verb. It is preferable to use the particle alone or a verb of doubt like 'сомневаюсь'. Another option is 'не думаю, что он придёт', but be careful: 'не думаю' can be more emphatic.

examples.translation: Quizás me quede en casa.
examples.note: The particle 'пожалуй' is placed at the beginning or after the subject, and expresses a tentative decision, often with the future tense.

examples.translation: Difícilmente sea verdad.
examples.note: 'Вряд ли' is used with the indicative and expresses high improbability. It does not use the subjunctive, unlike in Spanish.

examples.original: Едва ли они успеют к сроку.
examples.translation: Apenas llegarán a tiempo.
examples.note: 'Едва ли' is more literary than 'вряд ли' and is often used with perfective verbs.

examples.translation: Me parece que es una idea interesante.
examples.note: 'Мне кажется' is the most common way to say 'it seems to me'. It can be used in the past: 'мне казалось'.

examples.translation: Cabe destacar que los resultados son ambiguos.
examples.note: Impersonal verbs like 'следует' + infinitive give an objective and distant tone, very useful in academic contexts.

examples.translation: Se podría suponer que se equivocó.
examples.note: 'Можно + infinitive' is equivalent to 'one can/could' and serves to soften a statement without committing oneself.

examples.original: Я хотел бы сказать, что это не так.
examples.phonetic: [jæ ˈxətʲɪl bɨ skɐˈzatʲ | ʂtə ˈɛtə nʲɪ tak]
examples.translation: Me gustaría decir que no es así.
examples.note: The conditional with 'бы' softens the verb ('хотел бы') and expresses an opinion politely.

examples.translation: Valdría la pena discutir este tema.
examples.note: 'Стоило бы' + infinitive, literally 'it would cost', is used for cautious suggestions.

examples.original: Если бы я был на твоём месте, я бы подождал.
examples.phonetic: [ˈjeslʲi bɨ ja bɨl nɐ tvɐˈjɵm ˈmʲesʲtʲɪ | ja bɨ pədɐˈʐdal]
examples.translation: Si yo estuviera en tu lugar, esperaría.
examples.note: This construction with 'если бы' expresses counterfactual hypotheses, similar to the imperfect subjunctive in Spanish.

title: Глагольные управления с двумя дополнениями / Verb patterns with double object
bridge: In Spanish, many verbs that govern double objects (e.g., 'dar', 'enviar') use fixed prepositions ('a', 'para') and the order of complements is flexible. In Russian, double objects are expressed through grammatical cases (accusative, dative, instrumental, prepositional), and the choice of case depends on the specific verb. A common mistake is transferring the Spanish structure 'dar algo a alguien' to Russian by using only the accusative and dative, but some verbs require the instrumental or prepositional case. Additionally, while word order in Russian is more flexible, changing it can alter emphasis, whereas in Spanish the order is more rigid.
rule: In Russian, verbs with double objects are constructed with two complements that may be in different cases, depending on the verb. The most common patterns are: 1) Accusative (direct object) + Dative (recipient): дать (to give), послать (to send), подарить (to gift), показать (to show), объяснить (to explain). Example: Я дал книгу брату. 2) Accusative + Instrumental (instrument or agent with certain verbs): считать (to consider), называть (to call/name), делать (to make, when meaning 'to turn into'). Example: Они считают его гением. 3) Accusative + Prepositional (with prepositions о/об, про, в, на): говорить (to talk about), думать (to think about), рассказывать (to tell about), напоминать (to remind of). Example: Мы говорили о фильме. 4) Dative + Prepositional: участвовать (to participate in), нуждаться (to need). Example: Он нуждается в помощи. 5) Dative + Instrumental: владеть (to possess, to master) is not a double object, but увлекаться (to be interested in) is: Он увлекается музыкой. Additionally, some verbs govern the dative for the direct object (to help: помогать + dative, to call: звонить + dative). For C1 level, it is crucial to learn the cases governed by each verb, often memorizing lists and paying attention to verbs that change meaning depending on the case (например: смотреть на (to look at) vs. смотреть за (to look after)). Be mindful of verbs that are transitive in Spanish but require the dative or instrumental in Russian, such as 'ayudar' (помогать + dative) or 'interesar' (интересовать + accusative, but 'interesarse por' = интересоваться + instrumental).

concept_examples.text: Она подарила мне цветы.
concept_examples.translation: She gave me flowers.

concept_examples.text: Мы считаем его лучшим другом.
concept_examples.translation: We consider him our best friend.

concept_examples.text: Он рассказал нам о своей поездке.
concept_examples.translation: He told us about his trip.

concept_examples.text: Я помог брату с домашним заданием.
concept_examples.translation: I helped my brother with his homework.

common_error.explanation: The error occurs because the Spanish verb 'ayudar' is constructed with a direct object ('ayudo a mi hermano'), and the student transfers this structure to Russian using the accusative case. However, the Russian verb 'помогать' governs the dative case (¿to whom? → брату). To avoid this, it is essential to memorize the cases governed by common verbs and practice with lists of verbs that deviate from Spanish intuition. Pay attention to the question asked with each verb: 'ayudar' → 'помогать кому?' (dative).

examples.translation: She gave me a book.
examples.note: The direct object (книгу) is in the accusative case, and the recipient (мне) is in the dative. The order can vary: 'Она дала книгу мне' would change the emphasis.

examples.translation: We sent a letter to our parents.
examples.note: The dative case (родителям) indicates the recipient. In Spanish, 'a' is used with a person; in Russian, the dative case is used without a preposition.

examples.translation: Show me your new house.
examples.note: The verb 'показать' (to show) governs the accusative case (дом) and the dative case (мне). This is a fixed pattern.

examples.translation: They consider him a genius.
examples.note: The verb 'считать' (to consider) uses the accusative case for the person (его) and the instrumental case for the attribute (гением). In Spanish, 'considerar' is constructed with 'como' or an attribute; here, the difference lies in the case.

examples.translation: We appointed him as director.
examples.note: The verb 'назначить' (to appoint) governs the accusative case (его) and the instrumental case (директором). No preposition is used.

examples.translation: She found him drunk.
examples.note: The verb 'найти' (to find) can use accusative + instrumental to describe a state. This is an advanced usage.

levels.label: Глаголы, требующие дательного и творительного падежей
levels.translation: Verbs requiring dative and instrumental cases

examples.translation: He is passionate about painting.
examples.note: The verb 'увлекаться' (to be passionate about) governs the instrumental case (живописью). In Spanish, the preposition 'por' is translated into the instrumental case without a preposition.

examples.translation: We are interested in Russian history.
examples.note: The verb 'интересоваться' (to be interested in) governs the instrumental case (историей). In Spanish, it is 'nos interesa', but in Russian it is 'interesarse por'.

examples.translation: She needs help.
examples.note: The verb 'нуждаться' (to need) governs the prepositional case with 'в' (in). In Spanish, it is a transitive verb, but in Russian it uses 'в' + prepositional.

examples.translation: We will help you with the move.
examples.note: The verb 'помочь' (to help) governs the dative case (тебе) and optionally the instrumental case with 'с' (with). This is a double pattern.

title: Нюансы вида и времени / Aspectual nuances between verb tenses
bridge: In Russian, verbal aspect (perfective/imperfective) is a mandatory and systematic category, while in Spanish the distinction is expressed through compound tenses, periphrases, or simply context. A common trap is using the Russian imperfective aspect where Spanish uses the indefinite past, or vice versa. Remember that aspect is not tense: the same tense can have perfective or imperfective aspect. The choice depends on whether the action is viewed as completed, in progress, repeated, or as a result.
rule: In Russian, verbs come in aspectual pairs (совершенный вид – perfective, несовершенный вид – imperfective). The perfective aspect is used for completed, punctual, or resultative actions and does not combine with verbs expressing a process (estar + gerund). The imperfective aspect is used for actions in progress, habitual, repeated, or without emphasis on the result. In the past, the imperfective can correspond to the Spanish imperfect tense ('hacía'), but also to the preterite when the focus is on the process or duration. In the future, the perfective is a synthetic simple future (сделаю – 'I will do'), while the imperfective uses the auxiliary быть (буду делать – 'I will be doing' or 'I will do habitually'). Some verbs also have different meanings depending on the aspect (например: узнать – 'to recognize' vs. знать – 'to know'). For C1 level, it is crucial to master the nuances: the imperfective can indicate intention or a failed attempt in the past ('я убеждал, но он не согласился' – 'I tried to convince, but he didn’t agree'). There are also motion verbs with directional aspects (идти/ходить) that combine with prefixes to modify aspect and meaning.

concept_examples.text: Я писал письмо, когда он пришёл.
concept_examples.translation: I was writing a letter when he arrived.

concept_examples.text: Я написал письмо вчера.
concept_examples.translation: I wrote a letter yesterday.

concept_examples.text: Завтра я буду читать эту книгу весь день.
concept_examples.translation: Tomorrow I will be reading this book all day.
concept_examples.phonetic: [ˈzaftrə ja ˈbudʊ t͡ɕɪˈtatʲ ˈɛtʊ ˈknʲigu vʲesʲ dʲenʲ]

concept_examples.text: Завтра я прочитаю эту книгу.
concept_examples.translation: Tomorrow I will read this book (I will finish it).

common_error.wrong: Я писал это письмо вчера и отправил его.
common_error.correct: Я написал это письмо вчера и отправил его.
common_error.correct_alt: Я написал это письмо вчера и отправил его.
common_error.explanation: The error stems from transferring the Spanish simple past ('escribí') to the Russian imperfective 'писал', but in Russian, the context of 'writing and sending' implies that the action was completed and had a result, so the perfective 'написал' is required. The imperfective 'писал' in the past is used to describe the process or an unfinished action. To avoid this, identify whether the action has a clear result or a specific time limit; if so, use the perfective aspect.

examples.original: Он читал газету и пил кофе.
examples.translation: He was reading the newspaper and drinking coffee.
examples.note: Imperfective: describes simultaneous ongoing actions in the past, like the Spanish imperfect tense.

examples.original: Он прочитал газету и выпил кофе.
examples.translation: He read the newspaper and drank his coffee.
examples.note: Perfective: completed actions with a result, equivalent to the Spanish preterite.

examples.original: Я звонил ему, но он не отвечал.
examples.phonetic: [ja zvɐˈnʲil jɪˈmu no on nʲɪ ɐtˈvʲet͡ɕɪl]
examples.translation: I called him (tried to call) several times, but he didn’t answer.
examples.note: The imperfective 'звонил' indicates an attempt or repeated action; often used to express trying something without success.

examples.original: Завтра мы будем гулять в парке.
examples.translation: Tomorrow we will be walking in the park (ongoing activity or without emphasis on completion).
examples.note: Imperfective future with 'буду' indicates a continuous activity, similar to the simple future describing an ongoing action.

examples.original: Завтра мы погуляем в парке и вернёмся домой.
examples.phonetic: [ˈzaftrə mɨ pəɡʊˈlʲæjɪm f ˈparkʲɪ i vʲɪrˈnʲɵmsʲə dɐˈmoj]
examples.translation: Tomorrow we will walk in the park and return home.
examples.note: Perfective 'погуляем' indicates that the action will have a result or be completed; it is a synthetic simple future.

examples.original: Когда я вырасту, я стану врачом.
examples.translation: When I grow up, I will be a doctor.
examples.note: Perfective 'стану' signals a completed state change, while 'буду' would be more for a continuous situation.

examples.translation: I have known him for a long time.
examples.note: Imperfective 'знать' – to know as a state.

examples.translation: I recognized him immediately.
examples.note: Perfective 'узнать' – to recognize (a punctual action of coming to know).

examples.original: Он уговаривал меня, но я отказался.
examples.translation: He was trying to convince me, but I refused.
examples.note: Imperfective 'уговаривать' expresses a continuous attempt; the perfective 'уговорить' would imply success.

examples.translation: He convinced me to go.
examples.note: Perfective indicates that the persuasion was successful.

title: Пассивные конструкции с неопределённо-личным значением / Advanced passive constructions
bridge: In Spanish, expressions like 'se cree que' or 'se dice que' are formed with the impersonal 'se' + verb, or with structures like 'es sabido que'. In Russian, the natural equivalent uses the predicative adverb 'известно', 'сообщается' or the particle 'бы' with the infinitive, but it also employs the dative with the infinitive to express personal opinion (e.g., 'мне кажется'). The main trap is that Spanish speakers tend to incorrectly use the reflexive 'себя' or translate 'se dice' as 'оно говорится', which is ungrammatical. Additionally, Russian uses the instrumental case in passive constructions with the agent, something that has no direct parallel in Spanish.
rule: In Russian, advanced passive constructions are formed in several ways: (1) verbs ending in -ся with passive meaning (e.g., 'сообщается' - it is reported), restricted to imperfective or perfective verbs without a direct object; (2) short passive past participles with the verb 'быть' in the past (e.g., 'было сообщено'); (3) impersonal constructions with predicative adverbs like 'известно', 'нужно', 'возможно' + infinitive or clause with 'что'; (4) to express 'se cree que', 'считается, что' is frequently used (with dative if there is a person: 'мне считается' is incorrect, but 'я считаю' is active). In formal contexts, the dative + infinitive is used to express opinion, e.g., 'мне кажется' (it seems to me). The agent in passive constructions is marked with the instrumental case: 'Книга была прочитана студентом' (The book was read by the student). For 'se dice que', the impersonal form is 'говорят, что' (no reflexive). Avoid using 'себя' as a passive. At the C1 level, students are expected to use these structures in academic and journalistic registers and distinguish between passives with and without an explicit agent.

concept_examples.text: Считается, что экономика растёт.
concept_examples.translation: It is believed that the economy is growing.

concept_examples.text: Сообщается, что президент подписал указ.
concept_examples.translation: It is reported that the president signed the decree.

concept_examples.text: Известно, что это здание было построено в XIX веке.
concept_examples.translation: It is known that this building was constructed in the 19th century.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɪzˈvʲɛsnə | ʂto ˈɛtə ˈzdanʲɪje ˈbɨlə pɐˈstroɪnə f dʲɪvʲɪˈnɒtsətəm ˈvʲɛkʲe

concept_examples.text: Считается, что он лучший врач в городе.
concept_examples.translation: It is said that he is the best doctor in the city.
concept_examples.phonetic: ɕːɪˈtaɪtsə | ʂto on ˈlut͡ʃɨj ˈvrat͡ɕ v‿ˈɡorədʲe

common_error.wrong: Оно говорится, что погода будет хорошая.
common_error.explanation: The error arises from translating 'se dice' literally as 'оно говорится', using 'оно' as an impersonal subject. In Russian, the impersonal is expressed with the third-person plural without a subject ('говорят') or with the verb ending in -ся ('сообщается'). 'Оно' is not used as a dummy subject; Russian has no equivalent of 'ello'. To avoid this error, remember that Russian impersonal constructions do not have an explicit subject, and the verb ending in -ся already conveys the passive nuance.

examples.translation: It is reported that the meeting is postponed.
examples.note: The verb 'сообщаться' is impersonal and does not take a subject; the action is expressed with the clause 'что'. Unlike Spanish, the reflexive 'se' is not used.

examples.translation: It is expected that everyone will be present.
examples.note: 'Полагается' expresses impersonal expectation; in Spanish we use 'se espera' or 'se supone', but in Russian the verb ending in -ся does not admit a subject.

levels.label: Считается, что / Известно, что
levels.translation: It is believed that / It is known that

examples.translation: It is considered that this film is a masterpiece.
examples.note: In this construction, 'считается' functions as impersonal; the focus is on general opinion, not the speaker.

examples.translation: It is known that he wrote the thesis.
examples.note: Here 'известно' is a predicative adverb, not a verb; it is invariable and requires a clause with 'что'. In Spanish, the structure is parallel with 'es sabido que'.

examples.translation: It seemed to me that he was right.
examples.note: The construction 'мне казалось' uses the dative for the person perceiving; in Spanish we use 'me parecía', also with an indirect object pronoun.

examples.original: Ему суждено было стать великим учёным.
examples.phonetic: jɪˈmu sʊˈʐdɛnə ˈbɨlə statʲ vʲɪˈlʲikʲɪm ʊˈt͡ɕɵnɨm
examples.translation: He was destined to become a great scientist.
examples.note: This impersonal passive with dative + short participle expresses destiny; in Spanish 'estaba destinado' + infinitive is used, similar but with a subject.
